question: The Melchizedek priesthood. What does that power actually do for you?
intro: Melchizedek shows up in three verses of Genesis. He's a king and a priest. Abraham pays him tithing. Then he's gone. And somehow the highest priesthood in the Church is named after him. Hebrews spends a whole chapter on him. Alma spends half of one. If you've ever held or been blessed by that priesthood and wondered what that power actually does, this is the week.

days.q: What does the Bible say about him?
days.intro: Read the three verses in Genesis. That's all the Old Testament gives you about the man. Then read what priesthood looks like in action: Peter at the temple gate with a man who'd begged there his whole life. When you read, notice what Peter says he *does* have.
days.journal: What do you actually know about the priesthood? Not the definition. What it does. Write it down before this week.

days.q: What did Melchizedek actually do with it?
days.intro: Alma tells you more about Melchizedek than the whole Bible does. He was king over a city full of wickedness. He preached repentance, the people actually repented, and the place became known for peace. That's what priesthood is for. Then D&C 107 tells you why the priesthood carries his name. When you read, look at what changed in the people, not in him.
days.journal: When has a priesthood blessing or ordinance actually brought you peace? If you can't think of one, who could you ask for one this week?

days.q: What does the Restoration add?
days.intro: The Restoration tells you what the priesthood *does*, and it's bigger than passing the sacrament. D&C 107 says it holds the keys to every spiritual blessing of the Church, even to have the heavens opened. D&C 84 says without its ordinances the power of godliness doesn't show up. When you read D&C 84:19-22, slow down. That's the whole point in four verses.
days.journal: D&C 84:20 says the power of godliness shows up in the ordinances. What's an ordinance where you've actually felt that? What was it?

days.q: What does an apostle say about keys and authority?
days.intro: President Dallin H. Oaks, April 2014. He explains keys, authority, and who has what, including a section on women and priesthood authority that surprised a lot of people.

read.talk: The Keys and Authority of the Priesthood
read.speaker: Dallin H. Oaks

days.takeaway: His point is that priesthood keys are what direct the use of priesthood power, and they're held by a few people so the power can be used by many. He says something most members haven't heard: when a woman is set apart under the direction of someone with keys, she exercises priesthood authority in that calling. The priesthood isn't a men's club. It's God's power, organized, and everyone in the Church operates under it.
days.journal: Oaks says anyone set apart exercises priesthood authority in their calling. Does that change how you see your own calling, or someone else's?

days.q: If Jesus is the high priest, why do we need any others?
days.intro: Here's the hard part. Hebrews says Christ is the only high priest we need, forever. So why does the Church ordain thousands of men? Isn't that exactly the Levitical system Hebrews said was replaced? Read Hebrews again, carefully. Then read D&C 121 on how fast the priesthood stops working when it's misused. Then read the Lord's own explanation of why He gives power to men at all.
days.journal: D&C 121:37 says the priesthood quits working the moment it's used to control someone. Have you ever seen that happen? What did it look like?

days.q: How is it supposed to be used?
days.intro: D&C 121 is the answer, and it's the opposite of what most people expect from the word "authority." Persuasion. Long-suffering. Gentleness. Love unfeigned. Then read the oath and covenant, which is what you sign up for when you receive it. When you read, list what the priesthood is *not* allowed to do.
read: Preach My Gospel, lesson 5, "Priesthood and Auxiliaries"
days.journal: Whether you hold the priesthood or are blessed by it, pick one thing from D&C 121:41-42 to do this week. Not think about. Do.

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to Melchizedek. Read Genesis 14 one more time, then Peter at the temple gate. Then read your Day 1 answer.
days.journal: Answer the week's question: What does the Melchizedek priesthood actually do for you? And what do you know about it now that you didn't on Day 1?

question: Faith without works is dead. But we're saved by grace. Pick one?
intro: Paul says you're saved by faith, not works. James says faith without works is dead. Martin Luther wanted James thrown out of the Bible over it. We tend to like James and get nervous around Paul. Neither one is wrong. But if you can't explain how both are true, you'll spend your life bouncing between earning your way and coasting. This week is Week 30 finished.

days.q: What did James actually say?
days.intro: Read James 2. He's blunt: show me your faith without works and I'll show you mine by them. He uses Abraham and Rahab as examples, and here's the thing: Paul used Abraham too, to prove the opposite point. Same guy. When you read, notice James isn't against faith. He's against a certain kind of "faith."
days.journal: Read your Week 30 Day 7 answer next. Then write: do you lean Paul or James? Which one makes you nervous?

days.q: Were Paul and James actually disagreeing?
days.intro: Paul quotes Genesis 15, where Abraham believed and it was counted as righteousness. James quotes Genesis 22, where Abraham offered Isaac. Same man, thirty years apart. Paul is answering "how do you get in?" James is answering "how do you know you're in?" Read both of them using Abraham, then read Genesis, and see whether they're fighting or describing two ends of the same thing.
days.journal: Paul's Abraham believed. James's Abraham obeyed. Was that one faith or two? What did the thirty years in between do?

days.q: What does the Book of Mormon say works are for?
days.intro: Amulek says your prayer is worthless if you turn away the needy. Moroni says a work done without real intent counts as nothing. King Benjamin says even serving God your whole life leaves you in debt. Put those three together and you get the answer: works don't buy anything. They *show* something. When you read, look for what the works are evidence of.
days.journal: Moroni 7 says a gift given grudgingly is counted as if you kept it. What's something you do for God grudgingly? What would it take to do it for real?

days.q: What does an apostle say about the order?
days.intro: President Dieter F. Uchtdorf, October 2018. Three words in the title, and the order of the three words is the whole talk.
days.takeaway: His point is that the sequence matters. You believe, that changes what you love, and what you love changes what you do. Works come *out* of faith, not in front of it. He says if you try to do without believing, you burn out. If you believe without doing, you were never really believing. The doing is the proof that the believing was real.
days.journal: Uchtdorf says believe, then love, then do. Where does your discipleship usually start? Is it in the right order?

days.q: Can you have real faith and still not act?
days.intro: Here's the hard part. James says no. But you've had faith and still not acted, and you know it wasn't fake. So what's going on? Jesus says if you love Him, keep His commandments, which sounds like James. John says if you say you know Him and don't keep them, you're lying. But the Lord also warns about doing things only because you're commanded. Read these and figure out where laziness ends and dead faith begins.
days.journal: Where's the line between "I have faith but I'm being lazy" and "my faith is dead"? Which side are you on with the thing you've been avoiding?

days.q: What works, specifically?
days.intro: Not a checklist. The resurrected Christ said the works are the ones you've seen *Him* do. Matthew 25 lists them. James says be a doer of the word, not just a hearer, and describes what a hearer-only looks like. When you read, look for the works that count. They're not impressive.
read: Preach My Gospel, lesson 3, "Faith in Jesus Christ" and "Endure to the End"
days.journal: Pick one work from Matthew 25:35-36. Do it this week for a specific person. Write who and what. That's your faith made visible.

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to James 2. Read it one more time. Then read your Day 1 answer and your Week 30 answer side by side.
days.journal: Answer the week's question: Faith or works? Say how both are true in a way that would satisfy Paul *and* James.

question: "If any of you lack wisdom." What did Joseph Smith actually do with that verse?
intro: A fourteen-year-old farm kid read one verse in James and it started the Restoration. Millions of people have read the same verse and nothing happened. So what did Joseph do that they didn't? The verse says ask God. Everybody asks God. But Joseph did something specific with it, and Preach My Gospel builds the whole first lesson on it. This week is about the verse, the boy, and the method.

days.q: What does James say, and what did Joseph do with it?
days.intro: Read James first. Then read Joseph's own account of reading it. When you read Joseph, pay attention to what he says the verse did to him and what he did *next*. There's a gap between reading and asking, and what he did in that gap is the whole story.
days.journal: Joseph says the verse entered his heart with great force. Has any scripture ever done that to you? Which one?

days.q: What was James actually promising?
days.intro: James was Jesus's brother. He wrote to Jews scattered across the empire, practical people. "Wisdom" in Greek is *sophia*, practical wisdom, knowing what to do. And "upbraideth not" means God won't scold you for asking. Read the verses in James about asking without wavering. That's the condition. It's not "ask nicely." It's "ask like you'll act."
days.journal: "Upbraideth not." God won't scold you for asking. What question have you not asked because you were embarrassed to?

days.q: What happened when he asked?
days.intro: Read the First Vision in Joseph's own words. All of it, including the part before the light, which people skip. He was attacked first. Then read the Lord telling Oliver Cowdery that he'd already received an answer he hadn't recognized. Two ways answers come. When you read, notice what Joseph did when the darkness hit.
days.journal: Joseph was nearly overcome before the light came. Have you ever been closest to giving up right before an answer? What happened?

days.q: What does the prophet say about it?
days.intro: President Russell M. Nelson, April 2020, the 200th anniversary of the First Vision. He's talking about what the Father said in the grove and what it means for you.
days.takeaway: His point is that the Father said one thing in the grove that matters for everyone: "Hear Him." Not "hear about Him." Hear Him. Nelson says the First Vision isn't just history, it's the pattern: you have a question, you go somewhere to ask it, and God answers. And he says the most important thing you can do in your life is learn to hear the Lord's voice, because it's not optional for what's coming.
days.journal: Nelson says learn to hear Him. When was the last time you'd say you heard Him, not just felt something? What did He say?

days.q: Joseph asked and got a vision. I ask and get nothing. So what's the difference?
days.intro: Here's the hard part. You've asked in faith. No pillar of light. Was Joseph special, or are you doing it wrong, or is there a third option? Read the Lord explaining to Oliver why his attempt to translate failed. Read the Lord on how *most* revelation comes. Read Alma's experiment, which promises a result but not a vision. Then be honest about what you were expecting.
days.journal: What were you expecting when you asked? A vision? A feeling? A voice? Would you recognize the answer if it came a different way?

days.q: How do you ask like Joseph did?
days.intro: Joseph's method is in JS-H 1:12-13 and it's specific: he read the verse, reflected on it again and again, concluded he had to ask, and picked a place and time. Moroni adds "real intent," which means you've decided to act before you get the answer. When you read, write down the actual steps.
read: Preach My Gospel, lesson 1, "Pray to Know the Truth through the Holy Ghost"
days.journal: Pick one question. Do Joseph's steps this week: read something about it, reflect on it again and again, decide to ask, pick a place, and go. Write the question and the place.

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to James 1:5. Read it one more time. Then read your Day 1 answer and your Day 6 question.
days.journal: Answer the week's question: What did Joseph do with that verse? And what did you do with it this week?

question: "Partakers of the divine nature." Can people really become like God?
intro: Peter says you can become a partaker of the divine nature. Paul says you're a joint-heir with Christ. John says when He appears we'll be like Him. Most of Christianity reads those as metaphors. We read them as the point. That gets us called heretics. This week is about what the scriptures actually say you can become, why early Christians believed it, and whether you actually believe it about yourself.

days.q: What did Peter say?
days.intro: Read 2 Peter 1. He says God has given you promises so that you can become a partaker of the divine nature, and then he gives a ladder of things to add to your faith. When you read, notice the order of the ladder. It starts with faith and ends with charity. Then read Paul on inheritance.
days.journal: "Partakers of the divine nature." Do you actually believe that's about you? Or does it feel like it's about someone more spiritual?

days.q: Did early Christians believe this?
days.intro: Yes. For centuries. The Greek fathers called it *theosis*, becoming like God. Irenaeus and Athanasius both said God became man so that man might become like God. It was mainstream. It faded in the West. Read where they got it: Psalm 82, which Jesus quoted to the Pharisees when they accused Him of blasphemy. Then John, who says we'll be like Him.
days.journal: John says when we see Him we'll be like Him. Where do you already look a little like Him? If you're stuck, ask someone who knows you.

days.q: What did the Restoration reveal?
days.intro: D&C 76 is Joseph Smith's vision of the kingdoms of glory, and the description of the celestial kingdom says the words nobody else will: they are gods, even the sons of God. Read it. Then D&C 132, on what exaltation means, and Moses 1:39, which tells you what God is *for*. When you read, notice how much of it is about relationships, not power.
days.journal: D&C 76:58 says "they are gods." What's your gut reaction reading that? Excitement, fear, disbelief? Why?

days.q: What does the prophet say about thinking that way?
days.intro: President Russell M. Nelson, October 2023. He says two words that became a slogan, and the talk behind them is about exactly this.
days.takeaway: His point is that every decision you make should be run through one question: what does this mean for my eternal life? He says thinking celestial changes how you handle conflict, temptation, and grief, because you're not living for this life. And he says the doctrine that you can become like God isn't a distant fantasy, it's the reason the commandments exist. They're how you get there.
days.journal: Nelson says run decisions through "what does this mean for eternity." Pick one decision you're facing. Run it through. What changes?

days.q: Isn't this blasphemy?
days.intro: Here's the hard part. Isaiah has God saying there was no God formed before Him and won't be after. Christians hear "you can become a god" and think we're demoting God. So what does exaltation actually claim? Read Isaiah. Then read how the Lord describes the relationship between Father and Son and us, which is the model. Then decide: does becoming *like* Him mean becoming *instead of* Him?
days.journal: What would you say to a Christian friend who says this doctrine makes God smaller? Write your actual answer.

days.q: How do you become that?
days.intro: Peter gave you the ladder on Day 1. Read it again as instructions: add to your faith virtue, to virtue knowledge, and on up. The resurrected Christ asks the question and answers it: what manner of men ought ye to be? As I am. Moroni tells you what to pray for. When you read, look for how ordinary the steps are.
read: Preach My Gospel, lesson 2, "The Kingdoms of Glory"
days.journal: Pick the next rung on Peter's ladder you need. Write it. Write one thing this week that's a step on that rung.

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to 2 Peter 1:4. Read it one more time. Then read your Day 1 and Day 3 answers.
days.journal: Answer the week's question: Can people really become like God? And do you believe it about *you*?

question: Was the Fall a mistake?
intro: Most of Christianity says Adam and Eve blew it. Original sin, the world broken, everything since is damage control. We say something different: the Fall was part of the plan. Eve was wise. Adam was right. If that's true, it changes everything about how you see yourself, your body, your struggles, and God. If it's not true, we've been telling ourselves a nice story. This week finds out.

days.q: What does Genesis say happened?
days.intro: Read the Garden story straight. Two trees, one commandment, one serpent. Then read the Book of Moses, which is Joseph Smith's revealed version, and notice what it adds: the serpent's motive, and who Satan actually is. When you read Moses, look for what the Bible left out.
days.journal: Before this week: was the Fall a mistake, a sin, a plan, or something else? Write your honest answer.

days.q: What did Adam and Eve face?
days.intro: They'd been given two commandments that couldn't both be kept. Multiply and fill the earth. Don't eat the fruit. In the Garden they couldn't have children. So one commandment had to give. Read Eve's reasoning, then read what Adam and Eve said *after* they'd been cast out. It's not what you'd expect from people who'd just ruined everything.
read: Genesis 3:16-19 (the consequences, which we call blessings in disguise)
days.journal: Eve said "were it not for our transgression we never should have had seed." Does that sound like regret? What does it sound like?

days.q: What does the Book of Mormon say the Fall was for?
days.intro: Lehi's explanation to Jacob is the clearest treatment of the Fall anywhere in scripture. Adam fell that men might be. Men are that they might have joy. Then Alma adds the word "probationary," which means the Fall created the test you're in. When you read, look for what the Fall made possible that wasn't possible before.
days.journal: 2 Nephi 2:25. Adam fell that men might be. Men are that they might have joy. Does your life feel like it was designed for joy? Why or why not?

days.q: What does an apostle say about opposition?
days.intro: President Dallin H. Oaks, April 2016. He explains why the Fall was necessary and makes a distinction between transgression and sin that clears a lot up.
days.takeaway: His point is that opposition isn't the enemy of the plan, it *is* the plan. Without it there's no growth, no choice, no joy. He says Adam and Eve's act was a transgression, breaking a formal rule, not a sin, doing something inherently wrong, and that the distinction matters because it means the Fall was a step forward, not a catastrophe. And he says your own opposition, the stuff you'd rather not deal with, is the same thing: the condition that makes becoming possible.
days.journal: Oaks says opposition is the plan, not the obstacle. What's the opposition in your life you've been treating as a mistake?

days.q: If God wanted them to fall, why forbid it?
days.intro: Here's the hard part. If the Fall was the plan, why did God command them not to eat? Was He setting them up? And if Eve was wise, why did she get deceived? Read the two commandments again and notice God said "nevertheless, thou mayest choose." Read Lehi on why there had to be a real choice. Then read the Lord telling Adam his children are innocent. Sit with whether God was tricking them or teaching them.
days.journal: Moses 3:17 says "thou mayest choose for thyself." Was that a trap or a gift? Write the case for each. Then pick.

days.q: What do you do with agency now?
days.intro: The Fall gave you a body, a test, and the ability to choose. Lehi says you're free to choose liberty or captivity. Samuel the Lamanite says you're your own judge. The Lord says don't wait to be told. When you read, look for what the scriptures say agency is *for*. It's not for getting away with things.
read: Preach My Gospel, lesson 2, "Agency and the Fall of Adam and Eve"
days.journal: D&C 58 says people who wait to be commanded are slothful. What's something good you've been waiting to be told to do? Do it this week. Write it.

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to 2 Nephi 2:25. Read it one more time. Then read your Day 1 and Day 5 answers.
days.journal: Answer the week's question: Was the Fall a mistake? And what does your answer mean for the hard stuff in your life?

question: "The Lamb slain from the foundation of the world." Was the Atonement plan B?
intro: Revelation calls Jesus the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world. Before the world. Which means the Atonement wasn't a rescue mission God came up with after the Fall went wrong. It was the plan from the start. That raises a question: if God knew we'd fall and had a Savior ready, was the Fall a setup? And what does it mean that you were in the room when the plan was made? This week starts December with the beginning of everything.

days.q: What does Revelation say?
days.intro: Read the phrase in Revelation 13, then Peter saying the same thing, then John's vision of the Lamb in heaven with everyone worshipping. When you read, notice the timing in each one. "Before the foundation." "Foreordained." It's never "after."
days.journal: The Atonement was planned before the earth. Does that make it feel more certain to you, or more like you were never really free? Write your first reaction.

days.q: What did "Lamb" mean to them?
days.intro: Every Jew hearing "Lamb" thought of Passover. A lamb without blemish, killed so the family could live. John the Baptist called Jesus the Lamb of God the first time he saw Him. Isaiah described the Messiah as a lamb to the slaughter 700 years early. Read them in order. When you read, notice how far back the lamb goes. Abraham told Isaac God would provide one.
days.journal: Abraham told Isaac "God will provide himself a lamb." What did Abraham know about the plan? What does that story do to you now?

days.q: What did the Restoration reveal about the council?
days.intro: The Book of Moses and Abraham let you into the room. God asks who He'll send. Two volunteer. One wants the glory. One says thy will be done. Read it. Then read Alma on people being called from the foundation of the world, and King Benjamin on the Atonement being prepared then too. When you read, notice that the Atonement, the Savior, and *you* were all decided in the same council.
days.journal: Abraham 3:27: "Whom shall I send?" Jesus said "here am I, send me." Nobody made Him. What does it change to know He volunteered?

days.q: What does an apostle say about the Lamb?
days.intro: Elder Jeffrey R. Holland, April 2019. He gave this on Easter and it's about the Lamb specifically, what the word means and what it cost.
days.takeaway: His point is that the sacrament is where the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world meets you, every week, and most of us treat it like a break in the meeting. He walks through what the lamb imagery meant across all of scripture, from the Garden to Revelation, and says the whole plan was always pointing at one Sunday afternoon on a hill. And he asks you to take the sacrament like you know that.
days.journal: Holland says the sacrament is where the plan from the foundation of the world meets you. Next Sunday, what will you do differently because of that?

days.q: If God knew we'd fall, was the Fall a setup?
days.intro: Here's the hard part. God knew Adam would fall. He had a Savior ready. So was there any real choice? Read what you wrote in Week 47 about whether the Fall was a trap or a gift. Then read Satan's proposal in the council, which was to remove the risk entirely. Then read Alma on why God can't do that. The answer to "was it a setup" depends on what you think agency is worth.
days.journal: Satan's plan was to guarantee everyone made it. God rejected it. Why is a guaranteed outcome worse than a risky one? Answer in your own words.

days.q: What do you do with a plan made for you before you were born?
days.intro: You were in that council. Paul says you were chosen before the foundation of the world. Jeremiah was known before he was formed. Joseph F. Smith saw noble spirits held back for the last days. That's not just prophets. When you read, look for what being "prepared from the foundation" asks of you now.
days.journal: You chose this before you came. What's one thing you'd do differently this week if you actually believed you signed up for it?

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to Revelation 13:8. Read it one more time. Then read your Day 1 and Day 5 answers.
days.journal: Answer the week's question: Was the Atonement plan B? And what does it mean that you were there when it was decided?

question: The war in heaven. Are we still fighting it?
intro: Before the earth there was a war. Not with swords. With ideas. A third of God's children chose Satan's plan and were cast out. You were on the winning side, which is why you're here. But Revelation says the dragon went to make war with the rest of her seed, which is you. So the war didn't end. It moved. This week is about what the war was over, and whether you know which side you're fighting on right now.

days.q: What does Revelation say happened?
days.intro: Read John's vision of the war. Michael and the dragon. A third of the stars. Then read *how* the winners won, because it's specific and it's not by force. When you read, find the two weapons in verse 11.
days.journal: Revelation 12:11 says they overcame by the blood of the Lamb and the word of their testimony. Do you have both? Which one is weaker in you?

days.q: What did other prophets see?
days.intro: Isaiah saw Lucifer fall and named his sin: "I will exalt my throne. I will be like the most High." Jesus Himself said He saw Satan fall like lightning. Jude mentions angels who didn't keep their first estate. Read them and put together who Satan was and what he wanted. It wasn't to be evil. It was to be in charge.
days.journal: Lucifer's sin was "I will." Five times. Where does "I will" show up in your life in a way that's about being in charge instead of being good?

days.q: What does the Restoration say the war was about?
days.intro: The Book of Moses tells you Satan's actual proposal: save everyone, no one lost, and give me the glory. It sounds generous until you read what it required. Read it, then D&C 29 and D&C 76, which describe the rebellion and what became of it. When you read, look for the word "agency." That's what the war was over.
days.journal: Satan's plan would have saved everyone. God's plan let some be lost. Why is God's better? Explain it like you're talking to a kid.

days.q: What does an apostle say about choosing sides?
days.intro: Elder Dale G. Renlund, October 2018. He takes Joshua's line, "choose you this day," and says the war in heaven is the same choice, over and over.
days.takeaway: His point is that the choice made in the council wasn't a one-time vote. It's the same choice every day: God's way, where you use your agency and might fail, or Satan's way, where someone else takes the responsibility and you never grow. He says a lot of people who chose right in heaven are quietly choosing the other plan now, by wanting God to just make decisions for them.
days.journal: Renlund says wanting God to just decide for you is Satan's plan wearing a nice outfit. Where are you asking Him to take away a choice instead of help you make it?

days.q: If a third was lost then, is that happening again now?
days.intro: Here's the hard part. A third of God's children rejected Him with a perfect view of the plan. What does that say about people who reject it here, with a worse view? And what about the people you love who've walked away? Read what you wrote in Week 47 about the Fall. Then read Lehi on how free you actually are, and Samuel on being your own judge. Then read the Lord's warning that Satan's war is aimed at *you* specifically.
days.journal: Someone you love has walked away. Does the war in heaven help you understand it, or make it worse? Write what you actually think.

days.q: How do you fight now?
days.intro: Same two weapons: the blood of the Lamb and your testimony. Paul lists the armor. And Captain Moroni's people had one thing that made them fight harder than the Lamanites: they knew what they were fighting for. When you read, look for what you're supposed to be defending. It's not abstract.
read: Preach My Gospel, lesson 2, "Pre-Earth Life" and "Agency"
days.journal: Pick one piece of the armor in Ephesians 6 you're missing. What's it protecting? What are you going to do about it this week?

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to Revelation 12:11. Read it one more time. Then read your Day 1 and Day 3 answers.
days.journal: Answer the week's question: Are we still fighting the war in heaven? And which side are you actually on this week, judging by what you did?
